title: Gemini 4 Carbon for Architectural Drawings: What It Sees on a Sheet
summary: See what Gemini 4 Carbon found and missed on architectural sheets, then follow a millwork question from a plan callout to a Revit or AutoCAD revision.
body_markdown:
On one kitchen elevation, Gemini 4 Carbon found all five cabinets. On a different drawing, it identified 21 of 30 callouts, missed nine, and marked nine things that weren’t callouts. Count its marks and you get exactly 30. A check against the total alone would have hidden every miss. Both drawings are published examples from COXIT’s architectural drawing evaluation.[See the two annotated sheets](https://coxit.co/blog/claude-fable-5-2-architectural-drawings/)


That difference matters when a millworker asks whether a counter stops at the last base cabinet or continues over an open bay. Finding the cabinet run is a start. Answering the question means following a reference from plan to elevation and finding the dimension that resolves the end condition. Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28 and opened it more broadly on November 10 for work that benefits from longer reasoning and verification. Its launch included the paid Gemini API and the Gemini app for Google AI Ultra subscribers.[Google’s Carbon release](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-carbon-now-available/)


## Gemini 4 Carbon for architectural drawing review


CaseVBench gave models complete drawing sheets and asked them to put boxes around features a reviewer would look for. On 119 pages from nine projects, Carbon earned **83% overall F1** , a score that accounts for both missed features and extra marks. It earned **99% for locating floor plans, 74% for cabinets, and 49% for countertops** . Argon earned 76% overall on the same set. Those are scores for finding and locating objects. Reading a counter’s length requires a separate dimension check.[CaseVBench results by object type](https://casevbench.com/)


For the millwork question, ask Carbon to find the views first. Give it the plan sheet, the referenced interior elevations, and the latest millwork detail. Request the sheet number, view number, and visible dimension for each possible endpoint. That gives the millworker something they can open and check. An answer like “the countertop continues” leaves them searching the set a second time.


## Use Gemini 4 Carbon to trace a casework detail across sheets


Suppose the elevation shows the counter spanning the open bay, while the plan dimensions only the cabinet run. Those drawings can agree. A dimension string ending at the last cabinet tells you the length of the cabinets. It leaves the overhang open. Ask Carbon to quote the dimension labels and describe what each arrow touches. If the detail gives the overall top length, the team can put that reference on the markup. If the end is still undimensioned, the precise question for the designer is how far the counter extends beyond the cabinet.


## Update the Revit model and AutoCAD detail in ArchiLabs Desktop


Once the designer confirms the endpoint, attach the approved markup in ArchiLabs Desktop. In Revit, select the counter and identify the cabinet faces that stay in place. In AutoCAD, select the detail and ask for the counter outline and its overall dimension to be revised together. Desktop works with the native project objects, so the reviewer can measure the revised top directly.[See the Revit and AutoCAD workflows in ArchiLabs Desktop](https://archilabs.ai/desktop)


The millworker can now follow the same dimension in the model, the elevation, and the detail. The marked-up source sheet also records why it changed, which is often the first question when the shop drawings come back.
